units.title: The info you process by hand

objectives.text: Break a recurring information flow down into trigger, action, and condition (what kicks it off, what happens, when not to run)
Tell apart a manual, a scheduled, and an event-driven pipeline and choose the type for the task
Build the path from manual to automatic: first run the manual pipeline as a draft and find the weak spot, then add conditions, a schedule, and notifications
Use the automation map to judge which task can be delegated to a pipeline and which one needs a human

checks.question: In the pipeline “you give a URL → Firecrawl scrapes → Claude analyzes → the result is saved to Markdown,” what is the trigger here?
options: Scraping the page with Firecrawl
You giving the article URL
The model analyzing the text
Saving the result to a Markdown file
checks.explain: The trigger is what kicks off the process. Everything else in the chain is action — the steps that come after the launch (u1, “Today's pipeline”).

checks.question: A pipeline processed the same article twice and hit the rate limit. Which of the three questions before building was left unanswered during design?
options: Trigger: what kicks off the process
Action: what should happen
All three were answered; it's just a service failure
Condition: when should it NOT run
checks.explain: Duplicates, rate limits, and errors are exactly the third question, condition. It defines when the pipeline should not run (u1, “Three questions before building a pipeline”).

checks.question: Every new email has to be classified and a draft reply prepared for approval. Which pipeline type fits?
options: Event-driven: runs when a new email arrives
Manual: you run it yourself when you remember
Scheduled: once a day on a schedule
This isn't a pipeline: it needs a human, not automation
checks.explain: The process is kicked off by an event — an email arriving — not by the clock and not by your decision. The lesson walks through this exact example as event-driven. The draft goes for approval, so the decision stays with a human (u2, “Three pipeline types”).

checks.question: Occasionally, once every couple of weeks, you need to break down an article you've come across. Which pipeline type is more appropriate here?
options: Scheduled: every morning, so nothing slips by
Event-driven: on every new message
Manual: you run it yourself when needed
None: automating irregular tasks is pointless
checks.explain: A manual pipeline fits irregular tasks best: the algorithm is already assembled, and you pick the moment to run it. A schedule fits regular tasks (u2, “Manual pipeline (today)”).

checks.question: You've come up with a pipeline for a weekly report. Where does the lesson suggest starting?
options: Set up the schedule right away so you never have to come back to the task
Pick the most advanced tool so you don't have to redo it
Run it manually, make sure the algorithm works, and only then automate the trigger
Start with notifications and add the processing steps later
checks.explain: If you automate an unverified algorithm, its mistakes will repeat on schedule too. So the manual run comes first, and automating the trigger comes later (u2, the tip at the end of “Concept”).

checks.question: The first run of the pipeline came out uneven: one part of the result was weak. How does the lesson suggest treating this?
options: As a rough cut: find the one spot that “sagged” and make it the upgrade point for the second version
As a sign that the prompt is bad and has to be rewritten from scratch
As a reason to add more sources right away so the weak spot gets lost
As a normal result that doesn't need touching
checks.explain: The first run is a rough cut. Its job is to show where the chain sags, not to deliver a perfect result. The one weak spot you find becomes the plan for the next version (u3, “Reflection” and practice step 4, “Rate it: what worked? what could be better?”).

checks.question: The manual pipeline already works reliably. Which of these does the lesson call the natural next step?
options: Rewrite everything from scratch in an automation tool
Hand the pipeline the choice of which decisions to make based on the results as well
Drop saving to a file, since the result is visible in the chat anyway
Add a condition, for example “if the article is under 500 words — skip”
checks.explain: The path to automatic goes step by step on top of a working manual pipeline: conditions, a schedule, notifications, connecting to other tools. There's no need to rewrite from scratch (u4, “Next steps: from manual to automatic”).

checks.question: Which of these tasks does the automation map leave to a human?
options: Information gathering: URL → summary → file
Decision-making
Content analysis: text → insights → report
Meeting breakdown: audio → transcript → tasks
checks.explain: Gathering and analysis are easy to automate; meetings and emails are medium. The map marks decision-making as hard and needing a human (u4, “Automation map: what to delegate next”).
